args.text:
Snags

Pull up a stool, I'll walk ya through it. First up, cut a string of snags apart. Give each snag a few good jabs with a carving fork, so the little beggars don't split on ya. Into the frying pan they go, cover 'em with boiling water, and let 'em cook fifteen minutes; drain 'em, back in the frying pan, and fry till they're brown as a lifesaver. Serve 'em up with fried apples. Now, plenty of people grill their snags same as bacon instead, with the apples bakin' in a pan underneath to catch all the drips. Bloody beautiful.

Boston Baked Beans

Right, the main event. Pick over one quart pea beans, chuck out any rubbish, cover 'em with cold water, and leave 'em to soak overnight. Come mornin', drain 'em, cover with fresh water, and heat 'em up slow (keep that water under boiling point, mind), and cook till the skins are just about ready to burst,—and here's the trick: take a few beans on the tip of a spoon and blow on 'em. Cooked enough, the skins'll split right open. Them test beans have to go in the bin, of course; they've done their job. Drain the lot, and tip the bean water out the back door, not down the sink. Don't ask me why, that's just how it's done.

Then ya get stuck into the pork. Scald the rind of three-quarters pound fat salt pork, scrape it, cut off a one-quarter inch slice and drop it in the bottom of the bean pot. Score the rind of the rest of the pork every one-half inch, makin' the cuts one inch deep. Beans go in the pot, and ya bury the pork in 'em, but leave the rind pokin' up out the top. Mix one tablespoon salt, one tablespoon molasses, and three tablespoons sugar; add one cup boiling water, and pour that over the beans; then top it up with enough boiling water to cover 'em. Lid on the bean pot, bung it in the oven, and bake it nice and slow for six or eight hours. Six or eight hours, mate! Take the lid off for the last hour so the rind goes brown and crisp as. Add water as ya need it, so the lot doesn't dry out. Heaps of people swear by throwin' one-half tablespoon mustard in with the seasonings, reckon it makes the beans easier on the gut, if ya get my drift. And if ya'd rather pork with a bit of lean through it, go easy on the salt.

Now, Boston Baked Beans have got a ripper of a name for themselves, and people put it all down to the clay bean pot, the one with the little top and the big fat bulgin' sides they're meant to be cooked in. Fair enough. But I'll tell ya what: just as beaut beans have been eaten plenty of times where the bean pot's gone and broke and some bloke's grabbed a five-pound lard bucket instead. Does the job, doesn't it?

Oh, and yellow-eyed beans? Dead beaut baked, too.
